body: After FIIs were allowed in (1992) the Sensex made a new high of ~4,600 in Sept 1994 (level approximate), but then spent about a decade going nowhere: it was below ~3,000 in 2001 and only sustainably cleared its 1990s highs in 2003-04. The 1993-96 primary-market boom saw thousands of small IPOs (often at par or small premiums, sold through merchant bankers to retail); many companies later vanished with the money - the government's 'vanishing companies' list ran to a few hundred names (exact counts unverified). Mid/small caps of that era were the worst hit; S. Naren cites 1994-2004 as the lost decade for overvalued mid/small caps and as the analogue for 2025-26 risk. What led in 1994: newly listed small companies, cement, steel, finance companies; what lagged: everything afterwards except, from 1998, IT/ICE stocks. Signals at the top: issuance boom with poor-quality issuers, retail oversubscription, regulatory laxity (free pricing introduced 1992). Lesson: a market can deliver near-zero returns for ~10 years after an issuance and valuation peak; the quality of what is being listed is a top indicator, and it rhymes with the 2024 SME IPO mania.

data.lesson: issuance quality as a top signal; decade-long flat returns possible

title: IPO boom, 'vanishing companies' and the 1994-2003 lost decade
